`†` crud/search ran on an incomplete corpus (import below 1000/1000 bundles or not run before it, or the ES index not drained); on Bulk Import and its search indexing, search did not return every resource it ingested · `‡` more than 1% errors or failed checks in that suite (on Bulk Import and its ingest, any resource not ingested; on its search indexing, a rebuild that did not complete or reported errors) · `⚠` contended host (postgres crud above 3 ms/call) or a backend container died · **bold** = best in its row, shown only when no leg in that row carries a marker or `(partial)` (on the Bulk Import ingest and search indexing rows, also only when every leg indexed the same way) · Bulk Import is resources/s through `$bulk-submit` into a fresh database, kick-off until the search index covers it, and its ingest and search indexing rows split that time (see the note below the tables); it is one asynchronous job, so its p95 is n/a · n/a = no result (reason in brackets)

Batch/Transaction Import row (suite `import`): **resources/s** = entries of the transaction Bundles that committed (k6 `bundle_size`) per second of the import scenario's own clock, which starts after k6 setup() has loaded the two seed Bundles (that time is in Leg health) — the unit upstream's report uses. Its p95 is **per Bundle**: one k6 iteration, the corpus fetch plus the transaction POST. k6's `http_reqs` is not used for import: it counts a corpus GET beside every Bundle POST. Bundles/s is in Leg health. Its resources/s is not comparable with the Bulk Import row's: committed Bundle entries per second of the k6 scenario, against resources until the search index covers them. k6 drives it with 20 concurrent clients.

Bulk Import ingest and search indexing rows (↳): the same `$bulk-submit` load as the Bulk Import row, split into the two times a user waits for. **Ingest** = resources ingested ÷ seconds from kick-off until the status manifest is final (the web UI then shows the submission as Completed), those seconds in brackets: how long loading the corpus takes. **Search indexing** = the time spent indexing that freshly loaded data. On Elasticsearch legs indexing runs during ingest, so its time is the ingest time (`N s (= ingest)`, DEFER_INDEXING=false); elsewhere it is the deferred rebuild after Completed, in seconds from Completed until HFS's deferred search-index rebuild has finished (HFS_BULK_SUBMIT_DEFER_INDEXING, the default); the Search check in the Bulk import table then confirms it is searchable. `+ N s rebuild` is a follow-up rebuild of the types the index rejected. No best is marked on either row when legs indexed differently. Both rows are in the Throughput table only (one asynchronous job: no p95; failed resources are in the Bulk Import Errors row).

### Bulk import (`$bulk-submit`)

Each leg loaded the corpus `import` loads (its 2 seed bundles and 1,000 bundles, converted to per-resource-type NDJSON) through `$bulk-submit`, in a fresh database served by a second HFS, after the search suite. **Ingest** is kick-off until the status manifest is final; **Index** is the search indexing that follows (followed in the second HFS's log); **Total** is both, and is what the Bulk Import row above divides the ingested resources by; the ingest and search indexing rows above show **Ingest** and **Index** on their own. **Index** reads `inline (during ingest)` when HFS indexed while ingesting, so that time is inside **Ingest**. **Search check** compares Patient and Observation totals and two indexed queries with the converted corpus. It counts the 3,349 seed resources the Batch/Transaction Import row's entries do not.

| Leg | Result | Resources ingested | Ingest | Index | Total | Search check |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `sqlite` | ✓ | 1,630,685/1,630,685 | 395 s · 4,125/s | 1,655 s | 2,050 s | ✓ Patient 1,000 · Observation 689,080 |
| `postgres` | ✓ | 1,630,685/1,630,685 | 385 s · 4,233/s | 1,923 s (failed) | 2,308 s | ✓ Patient 1,000 · Observation 689,080 |
| `mongodb` | ✓ | 1,630,685/1,630,685 | 755 s · 2,159/s | 1,454 s | 2,209 s | ✓ Patient 1,000 · Observation 689,080 |
| `sqlite-elasticsearch` | ✓ | 1,630,685/1,630,685 | 490 s · 3,327/s | inline (during ingest) | 490 s | ✓ Patient 1,000 · Observation 689,080 |
| `postgres-elasticsearch` | ✓ | 1,630,685/1,630,685 | 225 s · 7,235/s | inline (during ingest) | 225 s | ✓ Patient 1,000 · Observation 689,080 |
| `mongodb-elasticsearch` | ✓ | 1,630,685/1,630,685 | 366 s · 4,462/s | inline (during ingest) | 366 s | ✓ Patient 1,000 · Observation 689,080 |

Runners: github-agent1, github-agent2, github-agent6, github-agent8 (8 CPU / 23G each).

Result sizes differ across legs (Observation 564,051 – 689,080), so crud and search did not run on the same corpus.

`sql-run` is HFS's own suite (`.github/scripts/fhir-bench/k6/sql-run.js`, 10 VUs for 1 minute): `$sql-run` over the stored corpus, one resource type per view. Its rows are requests/s and rows/s (NDJSON lines returned); per-view numbers are in each leg's job summary. It runs after search and before insert.

`insert` is HFS's own suite (`.github/scripts/fhir-bench/k6/insert.js`, load shape in its header): single-resource `POST Patient` and `POST Observation` creates, each Observation referencing that Patient, so every request is one create and its throughput row is creates/s. It runs last, after search and after the result-size snapshot, so its resources are in neither, and it never carries `†` because it does not read the corpus.

_Per-leg detail (leg configuration, p50/p99 and checks, the result-size cross-check, search latency by query shape) is in each `Benchmark (<leg>)` job summary; raw files are in the `fhir-benchmark-<leg>-<run id>` artifacts._
